Friend
FREND
n. (rendering Hebrew rēa', 'ōhēb, and Greek philos)
From Old English frēond, the present participle of frēogan, to love — so that a friend is literally a loving one. The Greek keeps the same tie: philos belongs to the phileō family of affectionate love. The Hebrew 'ōhēb is likewise the participle of 'āhab, to love, and it is that word which gives Abraham his title, the friend — the lover — of God.

Biblical Definition

Friendship in Scripture is a covenantal bond with duties attached, not a mere congeniality. Proverbs gives its cost and its candour: “A man that hath friends must shew himself friendly: and there is a friend that sticketh closer than a brother” (Pro 18:24), and elsewhere, faithful are the wounds of a friend, but the kisses of an enemy are deceitful — so that a friend is defined partly by his willingness to say what will not be welcome. Its highest human form is David and Jonathan, whose souls were knit together and who made a covenant, Jonathan stripping himself of his robe and giving it to the man who would take his father's throne. Its highest form altogether is divine. Abraham “was called the Friend of God” (Jas 2:23), a title given in the same breath as his justification by faith. And the Lord Jesus grants the name to His disciples with a stated reason: “Henceforth I call you not servants; for the servant knoweth not what his lord doeth: but I have called you friends; for all things that I have heard of my Father I have made known unto you” (Joh 15:15). Friendship there is defined by disclosure — a servant is told what to do, a friend is told what is going on. And the measure of it is given two verses earlier: “Greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends” (Joh 15:13), spoken by One who was about to do it, and for those who would shortly forsake Him.

Webster 1828 Definition

One who loves, and in Scripture one bound by covenant affection with duties of faithfulness and candour; the title given to Abraham, the name Christ grants His disciples on the ground that He has disclosed the Father's mind to them, and a bond measured by the laying down of life.

FRIEND, n. 1. One who is attached to another by affection; one who entertains for another sentiments of esteem, respect and affection, which lead him to desire his company, and to seek to promote his happiness.

2. One not hostile; as, he is no friend to virtue. Also, a favorer; one propitious.

3. The word is the participle of the old verb to free or to love; a friend is a loving one.

4. In Scripture, a title of Abraham, who was called the friend of God; and of the disciples, whom Christ called friends because he had made known to them all things heard of the Father. James 2; John 15.

5. A term of address, sometimes of gentle reproof. Friend, how camest thou in hither, not having a wedding garment? Matt. 22. Friend, wherefore art thou come? Matt. 26.

Key Scripture

Proverbs 18:24 — "A man that hath friends must shew himself friendly: and there is a friend that sticketh closer than a brother."

John 15:13 — "Greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends."

John 15:15 — "Henceforth I call you not servants; for the servant knoweth not what his lord doeth: but I have called you friends; for all things that I have heard of my Father I have made known unto you."

James 2:23 — "And the scripture was fulfilled which saith, Abraham believed God, and it was imputed unto him for righteousness: and he was called the Friend of God."

Modern Corruption

Friendship with Christ is taken to mean familiarity that levels the difference between the Lord and His servants, while the corresponding warning — that friendship with the world is enmity with God — is quietly dropped.

expand to see more

Joh 15:15 has been read as though Christ had resigned His lordship in favour of companionship, and a great deal of contemporary devotional language follows — Jesus as a mate, a supporter, an affirming presence with no authority in the relation. The text will not carry it. He says ye are my friends, if ye do whatsoever I command you, in the very sentence, and He had washed their feet a chapter earlier while telling them plainly, ye call me Master and Lord: and ye say well; for so I am. The friendship He grants is not the abolition of the servant relation but its enrichment by disclosure. He still commands; He now also confides. Losing either half ruins it: a Lord who never confides makes a religion of bare duty, and a friend who never commands makes a religion of sentiment.

James, who records Abraham's title as the friend of God, is also the writer who states the sharpest antithesis in the New Testament on the subject: know ye not that the friendship of the world is enmity with God? whosoever therefore will be a friend of the world is the enemy of God. The two verses come from the same pen and the same understanding of what friendship is — an alliance of affection and interest. One cannot be an ally of two parties at war. This is why Proverbs makes candour essential to friendship and warns that he that walketh with wise men shall be wise, but a companion of fools shall be destroyed. Friendship is formative, and the biblical counsel is not to have fewer friends but to know what a friendship is doing to the man in it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew rēa' is a companion or neighbour; 'ōhēb, a loving one, gives Abraham his title. Greek philos is a friend in the affectionate sense, from phileō, and philia is the friendship James sets against the love of God.

expand to see more

Hebrew rēa' (H7453) — friend, companion, neighbour; the word in thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself (Lev 19:18) and in the wounds of a friend (Pro 27:6).

Hebrew 'ōhēb (H157, participle) — one loving; used in 2Ch 20:7 and Isa 41:8 of Abraham, my friend, literally my lover.

Greek philos (G5384) — a friend, one dear; used in Joh 15:13-15 and of the friend at midnight (Luk 11:5).

Greek philia (G5373) — friendship; occurring once, in Jas 4:4, the friendship of the world is enmity with God.

Greek hetairos (G2083) — a companion, comrade; the cooler word the Lord uses to Judas in the garden, Friend, wherefore art thou come? (Mat 26:50).

Usage

"Of human friendship and its duties: a friend that sticketh closer than a brother (Pro 18:24); faithful are the wounds of a friend (Pro 27:6); the soul of Jonathan was knit with the soul of David (1Sa 18:1)."

"Of friendship with God: Abraham was called the Friend of God (Jas 2:23); the LORD spake unto Moses face to face, as a man speaketh unto his friend (Exo 33:11)."

"Of Christ's friendship and its cost: I have called you friends (Joh 15:15); greater love hath no man than this (Joh 15:13)."
